summary: Intermittent 429s observed when mixing webhook callbacks with long-lived SSE sessions on dedicated pool
description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightMap reports intermittent 429s on their dedicated pool when their service simultaneously maintains long-lived Server-Sent Events (SSE) sessions and high-volume webhook callback flows. The errors appear as 429 responses from the API edge with throttle headers.

Impact:
- Several production customers are seeing degraded ingestion for a subset of requests (webhook callbacks) while long-lived SSE client sessions are active.
- BrightMap reports ~6-12% callback failure rate during midday traffic spikes; business impact includes delayed analytics and missed alerts.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated-012) in eu-west region.
- Prod traffic; mixture of interactive SSE streams (chat UX) + webhook-based batching callbacks to the ingestion endpoint.
- Model traffic: inference (mistral-7b) and embedding generation (emb-encoder-v2).

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Open 150 concurrent SSE connections using the customer client with keepalive ping every 35s.
2) Start a webhook callback fanout at ~300 requests/min to the /v1/callback endpoint from multiple worker hosts behind a NATed proxy.
3) Observe ~5-10% of webhook requests returning 429 over a 15-minute window; SSE connections remain healthy but some SSE starts are delayed.

Observed behavior:
- Edge returns 429 with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset in ~20-30s.
- Throttle scope appears to correlate with API key and IP NAT pool reuse.
- BrightMap notes spikes correlate with Kubernetes sidecar health-checks and occasional bulk webhook retries.

Expected behavior:
- Webhook callbacks should be isolated from long-lived SSE sessions where customer has configured route separation and priority classes.

Temporary mitigation requested by customer:
- Guidance on configuration to prevent webhook callback fanout from consuming burst tokens while SSE sessions are active.
- Recommendation on TTL/keepalive tuning and proxy connection pooling to limit token double-counting.
investigation_notes: 03/10 09:45 Support triage: initial hypothesis - burst accounting mixing long-lived sockets and short webhook requests triggers shared token exhaustion at edge layer.
03/10 11:00 Collected customer traces and X-RateLimit headers; observed repeated near-zero Remaining values across distinct routes but same API key.
03/10 13:20 SRE reproduced locally using a mixed load harness: long-lived SSE clients + short POSTs through pooled NATed proxies; reproduced ~7% 429s within 10 minutes.

03/11 08:10 Hypothesis refined: NAT pool IP reuse causes token bucket attribution to group, health-check pings counted against same key, and sticky route-weighting causes webhook path to inherit lower priority weight.
03/11 12:00 Ran targeted experiment: disabled keepalive probes from a subset of pods and saw webhook 429 rate drop by ~60% for the duration of the test.

03/12 09:30 Edge proxy team instrumented per-connection accounting logs and found websocket/SSE long-lived connections were still contributing to burst-window consumption under current burst-pool config.
Next steps: propose config changes (route isolation + dedicated burst pool for long-lived sessions) and schedule a limited rollback window for BrightMap to try configuration patch.
Also assess whether backfill of burst credits following TTL rollover is delayed due to refill epoch alignment with eu-west time drift.

resolution_notes: Mitigation in progress: Support recommended enabling per-route priority isolation and requesting a dedicated short-burst pool for webhook callbacks. Planned change window 2026-03-13 22:00 UTC. Permanent fix: edge proxy to treat long-lived SSE keepalive pings as exempt from burst accounting if keepalive interval > 30s and connection marked interactive; engineering ticket INT-33021 tracks implementation. Follow-up: monitor for 48 hours after rollout and collect rate-limit heatmap.
